title: 🎙️ Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling
description: Today we explore how Cariboo and rural BC communities create, preserve, and share culture — from festivals and community radio to digital archives and open-source arts tools. We're looking for stories where creativity meets technology in small-town contexts, and where local artists and storytellers are finding new ways to reach audiences beyond geography. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_description: Today we explore how Cariboo and rural BC communities create, preserve, and share culture — from festivals and community radio to digital archives and open-source arts tools. We're looking for stories where creativity meets technology in small-town contexts, and where local artists and storytellers are finding new ways to reach audiences beyond geography.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling' — how communities create, preserve, and share culture, with particular interest in the Cariboo and rural BC.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: medical and health research with no cultural angle; resource-economy stories with no cultural framing; wildlife and nature stories without a creative or community-media context; data centre and AI investment news; geopolitical conflict, war, and crime coverage; financial market stories.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. A Cariboo tie raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band: judge on the strength of the arts/culture/storytelling reporting first.
- 80-100: Excellent arts, culture, or storytelling journalism. Cariboo/Williams Lake arts news lands here (arts council grants, murals, local festivals, Indigenous film, community theatre, heritage programs, a Cariboo author or artist honoured) — and so does outstanding national or international cultural reporting with real depth.
- 55-79: Solid arts/culture/media journalism. Rural BC and Canadian cultural coverage, CBC Arts features, regional festivals, community media projects, heritage preservation, creative-economy stories, digital storytelling tools and platforms, community media tech (podcasting, streaming, local publishing), animation and film production. Most genuine cultural journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Mainstream entertainment-industry coverage with modest substance (awards-show results, film/TV/music business news, publishing trade news).
- 15-29: Tangentially creative — a tech feature touching media/publishing/streaming, or Cariboo civic news with no arts angle.

ANCHORS: 'Repatriated Tŝilhqot'in baskets arrive in Williams Lake from Brooklyn Museum' → 95. 'How a BC First Nation is digitizing its oral histories' → 80. 'CBC Arts: the quiet revival of small-town prairie theatre' → 68. 'Netflix reports Q3 subscriber growth' → 20.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] NGOs say Israel bombed a journalist and appeared to attack ambulances trying to aid her – explainer
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Journalist Amal Khalil was killed in April in what colleagues described as a sustained attack by Israeli forces. Rescuers attempted to dig her out of the rubble of a building that had been targeted by Israeli forces, who had also prevented them from providing life-saving assistance.

Beirut-based Guardian correspondent Will Christou explains how investigations by Human Rights Watch (HRW), Amnesty International and Legal Agenda show that Israel deliberately and directly attacked Khalil and her colleague Zeinab Faraj, with apparent knowledge that they were journalists. The organisations called for the attacks to be investigated as war crimes, while HRW called for states to halt arms sales to Israel and put targeted sanctions on Israeli officials responsible for ongoing crimes.

Deliberately attacking journalists is a war crime. Israel has killed at least 15 journalists in Lebanon and 210 in Gaza since 2023, according to the UN human rights office.

Israel said it 'regrets any harm caused to journalists', and that they were killed 'as part of a series of events' during which two Hezbollah military operatives were killed

  • Israeli strike that killed journalist in Lebanon was war crime, say rights groups

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘They take our water, our soil’: protesters fight ‘foreignisation’ as Javier Milei encourages land sales in Argentina
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The country’s far-right president is courting billionaire investors by removing a block on foreign ownership of land and natural resources

On 19 September, Marta Sahores, an 84-year-old chemistry professor and activist who has mobilised against mega-mining projects for more than two decades, took to the streets in Argentina. Alongside workers, retirees, students, Indigenous groups and human rights organisations, Sahores was there to protest against the country’s far-right president, Javier Milei. During the marcha de la bronca – the “march of anger” – protesters held signs reading, among other rallying cries, “The land is not for sale”.

Marching in Esquel, a town nestled in the foothills of the Andes in Chubut province, she also held up a sign defending the country’s water resources against what she called the government’s “handover” to investors.
